scope: All substantive 2018 and 2019 local 3Blue1Brown English transcripts, excluding qa3, qa4, and fourier-series-montage, plus three 2020 probability videos.
method: Read every transcript row, in order within each video, using timestamped prose. Recovered missing portions of truncated batches in subsequent reads. Findings concern narration, stated visual encodings, and narrated operations, not independently observed frames or editing. Times are approximate source-caption locators, not frame-verified measurements.
data_cautions: Caption text includes transcription errors; do not treat mathematical wording as independently checked fact. For instance Wallis appears as Wallace, and some math formulas lose superscripts or punctuation.
Basel has only 16 rows, several spanning minutes, so some supporting spans are broad even though all text was read.

Some rows have impossible or irregular timestamps: final punctuation rows in uncertainty-principle and better-bayes have end before start; differential-equations has a reversed interval near 21:46. Use approximate locators and verify against video before precision timing claims.

The narration reports visual actions, color roles, and simulations, but this read does not verify actual colors, camera trajectories, dwell times, synchronization, or the quality of individual rendered frames.
Medical/test figures in better-bayes are historical hypothetical teaching examples in the transcript, not present-day medical advice or validated clinical performance.

findings.claim: Openings usually establish a specific tension the viewer can want resolved: an unexpected result, a choice with competing intuitions, or a visual whose mechanism is hidden. The topic name alone is rarely the entire motivation.

evidence.observation: States the inverse-square sum, reveals pi squared over six, asks why pi belongs, and converts the question into brightness of a line of lighthouses.
Introduces blocks and counts three, 31, 314, and 3141 collisions before naming the pi pattern. A narrated wait for the final collision turns a count into a miniature reveal.
Carefully defines polar plotting, then asks why spirals, rays, gaps, and the counts 20 and 280 appear; immediately separates the prime-number mystery from plotting artifacts.
Asks which seller to choose when percentages and sample sizes disagree; gives an early provisional answer and promises to unpack its assumptions.
An unknown coin weight leads to the apparent contradiction of assigning probabilities to individual continuous values.

findings.limits: Not a universal spectacular cold open: divergence-and-curl begins with definitions; eulers-formula-dynamically begins with the derivative property; heat-equation opens with a previous-episode recap.

findings.claim: The narrator teaches the representation before relying on it, making the visual grammar part of the explanation. Axes, colors, positions, bars, and motions receive explicit mathematical meanings.

evidence.observation: Compares paired input/output planes, vector fields, and color mapping. Hue encodes direction, brightness encodes magnitude, and black marks zero; points imaginatively visit output space, acquire color, and return.
Defines the label, pink point, fixed unit sphere, inside/outside regions, and point at infinity. Warns that all visible positions represent unit quaternions despite apparent distances.
Defines the rod's spatial axis, temperature graph, time-dependent surface, and partial derivatives; distinguishes time drawn as an axis from time represented through animation.
Explains radius and radian angle, then constructs points 1,1; 2,2; 3,3 before any pattern interpretation.
Explicitly changes the reader's interpretation from bar height to bar area, then derives density units and continuous curves from finer buckets.

findings.limits: The transcript supports narrated encoding instructions, not a claim that all these encodings were visually legible in the rendered videos.

findings.claim: Visual actions are often the reasoning itself: preserve a quantity while transforming the setup, then read an easier result. The explanation repeatedly connects an operation to its mathematical consequence.

evidence.observation: Inverse Pythagoras licenses replacing one lighthouse with two without changing apparent brightness. Repeated circle doubling generates the line of lighthouses; the invariant carries the known value into the limit.
Outward projection stretches width and contracts height; similar triangles show reciprocal scale factors, explaining preserved area rather than merely asserting equal surfaces.
Rescaling velocities turns energy conservation into a circle and momentum conservation into a line. Their intersections determine the next collision state.
Reflecting the world while continuing the ray straight converts bounce counting into counting equal angular sectors.
Colors encode the counts on either side; a pivot switch exchanges one same-color point for another, proving count invariance, and a half-turn forces every point to switch sides.

findings.limits: Not every attractive motif has a physical mechanism: wallis-product explicitly retains lighthouses even though multiplying distances no longer has the earlier physical brightness interpretation.

findings.claim: Representations are chosen by the question they make easier, and switching representations is frequently the central intellectual move. The narrator explains why the switch earns its complexity.

evidence.observation: Derivative becomes local stretch rather than graph slope; fixed-point convergence becomes repeated contraction. The ending acknowledges that this representation can be clumsy for a whole function.
Moves from orbital positions to velocity vectors rooted at one point, obtains a circle, then reconnects its tangency directions to the ellipse construction introduced earlier.
A failed dot-product interpretation of coordinates motivates signed areas, which transform uniformly through the determinant and permit recovery of unknown coordinates.
A multiplication rule fails for probabilities but becomes exact for odds. The formula comparison is framed as a design choice with tradeoffs, not a uniquely correct notation.
Uses Euler's shifting conventions to argue that representational choices should serve a concrete problem rather than an abstract standardization dispute.

findings.claim: The common movement is concrete case to operational intuition to notation, with formulas presented as compressed descriptions of something the viewer has already done mentally. Quantitative detail is retained when it makes the mechanism precise.

evidence.observation: Builds winding and center-of-mass behavior before translating rotation into a complex exponential and averaging into an integral; then corrects normalization to obtain the actual Fourier transform.
Counts 200 farmers and ten librarians, then selected subsets, before writing the general theorem; switches counts to areas to make the diagram portable and continuous.
Neighbor averaging becomes a second difference, then a second spatial derivative. The formula is motivated by a local update rule.
Visualizes counting in steps of six, then 44, before naming residue classes, coprimality, and Euler's totient function.
Simulation anticipates the probability, then counting arrangements and multiplying independent probabilities produces the binomial expression and checks the numerical result.

findings.limits: This is an order of explanation, not a ban on early equations: pdes shows an equation before unpacking it; eulers-formula-dynamically starts from an equation and derives motion; Cramer's rule states prerequisite knowledge.

findings.claim: Pacing is explicitly managed around dependencies and cognitive load: promise a destination, announce a detour, narrow attention, recap what matters, then return to the original question. Long explanations are not uniformly slow; they alternate overview and local detail.

evidence.observation: Promises a necklace/topology connection, labels the sidestep, anticipates the viewer's concern that the puzzle was abandoned, then marks the sphere-to-division correspondence as the key observation.
Recaps the original signal, wound-up graph, and center-of-mass plot as a three-part construct, then later reassembles the full formula after all refinements.
Cuts to a two-dimensional cross-section for one scale factor, then explicitly reminds viewers why the triangle calculation was needed.
evidence.quote: Deep in the weeds like this, it's sometimes easy to forget why we're doing this.

evidence.observation: Calls boundary conditions a necessary detour, motivates why a PDE solution can fail to model the rod, and explicitly returns to the main route after fixing endpoints.
Invites lingering on the opening construction, spends time earning a generalization into complex outputs, and finally returns to the original physical heat problem.

findings.limits: These are rhetorical pacing instructions and approximate story locations; no unverified average shot length or actual pause-duration claims.

findings.claim: Audience interaction is usually cognitively specific: predict a result, justify a relation, run a small experiment, generalize a case, or compute a missing step. The viewer is assigned a mathematical role, not merely asked whether the content is interesting.

evidence.observation: After supplying the creative sphere construction, invites viewers to finish the proof; separately offers a pause for tangent-length equality.
Asks viewers to iterate a function on a calculator, think through graph-based stability, then predict what happens near the other fixed point.
Turns the second proof into five progressively dependent questions, from ring circumference to the final fourfold area relation.
Gives enough setup for the three-dimensional extension, then leaves the generalization to the viewer and explicitly locates learning in that work.
Requests a pause to explain why the blue/brown counts remain fixed before giving the pivot-exchange argument.
Asks viewers to explain why multiplying the amount of data concentrates the likelihood curve.

findings.limits: Frequent rhetorical questions also serve transitions, so do not count every question mark as a genuine exercise. pi-was-628 has much less active mathematical work than sphere-area.

findings.claim: A wrong first idea is often deliberately made plausible and then broken, so the eventual definition or correction answers a felt need. This is guided discovery with explicit counterexamples.

evidence.observation: The all-colors boundary test first looks like a 2D sign-change test, but subdivision fails; winding number is introduced specifically because it composes additively.
evidence.quote: being wrong is a regular part of doing math

evidence.observation: Tries extracting coordinates with transformed dot products, shows that general transformations do not preserve them, and uses the failure to seek something that transforms predictably.
Sine-wave decay and even a static line solve the interior PDE but fail the simulated boundary behavior, creating a concrete reason to introduce boundary conditions.
A useful small-prior multiplication approximation yields an impossible 100% prediction for a larger prior; that failure motivates replacing probability with odds.
Starts with two and three points, then an interior fourth point breaks the naïve picture and shifts attention to choosing a central starting line.

findings.claim: Visual intuition is repeatedly distinguished from proof, literal physics, and representational artifacts. The narration makes simplifications visible and often repairs them quantitatively or labels what remains unproved.

evidence.observation: Admits shortened vector arrows and scope restrictions; explains imagined fluid as an analogy for electric fields rather than an actual electric fluid.
Calls apparent stretching a projection artifact and reminds the viewer that all projected unit quaternions have the same actual magnitude.
Warns that observing a 2D slice of a 3D flow is different from truly two-dimensional turbulence, then uses vortex stretching to explain the dimensional distinction.
After the apparent conclusion, exposes an unjustified limit interchange, shows a counterexample grid, and cites dominated convergence plus ordering cautions to repair the argument.
Separates physical velocity from abstract state-space motion; warns about vector scaling; demonstrates inaccurate finite stepping before reducing the timestep.
Separates finite approximation from an infinite limiting statement, acknowledges convergence issues, and explicitly says the drawn rotation is slowed by ten.

findings.limits: Some deep technical repairs are deferred to external resources; it would be wrong to describe every video as a complete rigorous proof.

findings.claim: The quantitative/qualitative balance follows the explanatory goal. Numbers discriminate hypotheses or verify behavior; qualitative imagery explains what those numbers do. The videos do not consistently avoid computation or consistently derive every numerical result.

evidence.observation: Explicitly postpones computation in favor of meaning, then supplies only a geometric sense of dot/cross-product notation.
evidence.quote: I'm purposely delaying discussion of computations here

evidence.observation: Begins with qualitative swirling, mixing, and unpredictability, then presents the 5/3 scaling law without a full derivation; its role is an example of order in chaos.
After the geometric mechanism, computes the relevant arctangent and discusses its approximation error to explain why the integer collision count agrees.
Explicitly separates analytic solutions, qualitative understanding, and computation; ends with a small Python Euler-step procedure after discussing the phase portrait.
Sets mental numerical estimation as an objective, uses exact odds updates, and repeatedly compares them with concrete population counts.

findings.claim: Endings often extract a transferable way of thinking or open the next dependency rather than simply restate an answer. The puzzle is treated as a vehicle for reusable mathematical habits.

evidence.observation: Reflects on equivalence of definitions and decomposes apparent genius into habits acquired through experience.
Generalizes to higher dimensions and explains that geometric objects matter for the other problems they encode.
Repeats the transferable lesson of translating dynamics into geometry, then promises a richer second solution.
evidence.quote: I don't want you to come away just remembering a neat puzzle

evidence.observation: Draws a teaching lesson about hindsight and difficulty, then identifies the mathematical habit of finding invariants.
Treats the initial plotting whimsy as incidental but values the chain of questions because prior exploration makes later definitions familiar.
Ends by showing why maximum likelihood does not itself answer the purchasing question, motivating Bayes and density functions in the next part.

findings.limits: Several endings deliberately withhold completion: clacks is the puzzle installment; quaternions defers the 3D rotation application; its short sequel routes viewers to an external interactive tutorial.
